That night he went to a nearby command post and had people hold the Hengshan Road intersection to keep Scarlet Guard reinforcements out. He did not go into Kangping Road himself, for fear of being recognized, and went back to the mill. Geng Jinzhang said going into the compound was his own decision. Huang Jinhai said a few of them drove over once to look.

820: On December 31, the Extra-Urgent Order was printed and issued in the name of the Workers' General Headquarters. 821: Wang Hongwen did not go to Kunshan. He said later that the Second Regiment wanted to send 100,000 people in pursuit and he stopped them. He argued against pursuit, for grasp revolution, promote production. The Second Regiment still sent tens of thousands. WGHQ headquarters sent no one. This is Wang Hongwen's own account and Huang Jinhai's.
822: The game found no reliable record of what Wang Hongwen did at this rally.
823: The Urgent Notice was written by Red Guards and issued jointly by the Workers' General Headquarters and other organizations. The Chairman wrote on it, “these two documents are very good.” Making temporary workers permanent was suppressed as economism.
824: The January power seizure was carried out under Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan. Ma Tianshui came over to their side and ran Shanghai's industry for the next ten years.
825: The commune's committee members were agreed among the organizations and decided from above. There was no election. Li Xun says the Paris Commune principles were put aside the moment it came to setting up the new government.
826: Before dawn on January 30, Wang Hongwen sent tens of thousands from the Workers' General Headquarters into the streets to control the main roads. The Red Revolutionaries fell apart after that.
827: At the Chairman's wish, the Shanghai People's Commune was renamed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee.
828: Wang Hongwen told Huang Jinhai that this was Comrade Chunqiao's view, and Geng Jinzhang could be arrested.

831: Wang Hongwen was at the command post in a nearby factory. The man who linked arms with others to escort the captives onto the trucks was Huang Jinhai.
832: Wang Hongwen's wages were always paid by No. 17 Mill, less than 60 yuan a month when he was Vice Chairman. The investigation materials also say he took large amounts of light industrial goods. Both are in the record.
833: Wang Weiguo never took Wang Hongwen to dinner. After September 13, Wang Hongwen worked with Xu Shiyou to lure Wang Weiguo to the Jinjiang Hotel and arrest him.
834: There is still no reliable account of why the Chairman had him read the Biography of Liu Penzi.
835: In July 1974, the Chairman criticized Jiang Qing, Wang Hongwen, Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan and told them not to form a little faction of four.
836: On October 18, Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha without telling the other Politburo members and told the Chairman that Beijing now had a strong flavor of the Lushan Conference.
837: The Guangdong Provincial Party Committee organized hundreds of criticism meetings, and Zhao Ziyang instructed that answering back be allowed. That the materials reached Wang Hongwen is a game premise.
838: Wang Hongwen told the Shadian representatives that if the village kept the work team and the People's Liberation Army out, it would come to smashing the mud forts. Three weeks later, the army entered the village.

840: Wang Hongwen phoned Shanghai to step up war readiness and had the police and the militia draw up a “Plan for Preventing Counterrevolutionary Riots.”
841: On September 11, Wang Hongwen set up a separate duty office of the General Office of the Central Committee in Zhongnanhai and told the provinces to report major problems to people he named.

892: A Few New Rooms at WGHQ
894:
Who the Scarlet Guards were, and what they defended

What the Scarlet Guards set out to defend was the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee and the Party committees of the mills and bureaus, the Party's leadership at every level. For many older workers, the Party committee was what the Party looked like in their mill and their city. Joining the Party, being named a model worker, promotion, housing, all went through the Party committee. In their eyes, opposing the Municipal Party Committee meant opposing the Party. Before the summer of 1966 this view was common sense. The rebels were the minority.

The Scarlet Guards were organized with the Municipal Party Committee's help. According to Huang Jinhai, on November 19 Cao Diqiu received representatives of the conservative workers. On the 23rd a preparatory meeting in the conference room of the Yangpu District Party Committee chose the name “Shanghai Headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards,” and Cao Diqiu said the Municipal Party Committee supported them. Yang Shifa, head of the Organization Department, had Zhang Qi, director of the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions, deal with them directly and gave them Room 103 of the federation as an office. On December 6 they held their founding rally in People's Square, and Cao Diqiu and other top leaders of the Municipal Party Committee came to show support. History

Most Scarlet Guards were Party and Youth League members, model workers and shop-floor activists, with many skilled workers and old masters among them. They claimed up to 800,000 members. History The figure is the Scarlet Guards' own.

They joined for different reasons. Some wanted to protect production. When the machines stopped, less cloth and yarn came out, and they saw the rebels as people who had walked off the job. Some did what the Party committee said. The branch in their mill mobilized them, so they went. In every campaign so far, those who followed the Party committee had never lost out, and those who stuck their necks out had mostly been labeled rightists. Late in a campaign they might even join the Party, be promoted or get a raise. Some sincerely believed the Municipal Party Committee had been sent by the Party to lead Shanghai, and that if it fell, Shanghai would lose its backbone. Some joined because of rivals in the mill. Whoever led the WGHQ in a given mill, the Scarlet Guards' leader in that mill was often his opponent. Interpretation The first three motives follow Huang Jinhai's summary of the Scarlet Guards in Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5 (“Party and Youth League members, activists, old model workers,” “following the Party committee is obeying the Party, you won't lose out”). The fourth follows the same chapter, which says the Scarlet Guards' founders were “mostly the opposing faction's leaders in the units that founded the WGHQ.” Huang Jinhai was on the other side, and his summary tends to play down the Scarlet Guards' own agency.

Li Xun divides the conservatives into several kinds. One kind was model workers and Party and Youth League members who sincerely identified with the seventeen years after 1949. They had benefited after 1949 and felt deep gratitude to the cadres who had given them honors. After the January power seizure, most of them withdrew from the Cultural Revolution in practice and showed their disagreement through silence. Most of the Scarlet Guards' main leaders, Wang Yuxi, Chen Achun, Li Jianyu and Ma Ji, were of this kind. Another kind worked hard to keep up with events. After Mao Zedong came out in support of the rebels, they turned on their old side and made self-criticism after self-criticism about having been “misled.” They kept or even raised their political standing. The model worker Yang Fuzhen later became a district Party committee secretary and vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. Another kind changed banners after the January power seizure and declared themselves rebels, and never truly got along with the original rebels. And one kind simply followed whoever had power. History See Li Xun, “The Overlooked History, Taking Research on Cultural Revolution Conservatives Seriously.”

Li Xun also says most ordinary people at the bottom joined the conservatives for safety. They had learned this from earlier campaigns. Before October 1966 the Center's position was unclear, and the safest choice was to keep following the cadres still in office. Later, when the rebels gained the upper hand, many people could not make sense of the situation and did not want to join the rebels either, so they stayed on the sidelines. Interpretation See the same article.

What the conservatives defended was the order and values formed after 1949. This differs from conservatism in the political-science sense. They accepted class struggle. What they opposed was an overly fierce drive to overthrow everything. Among the activists who raided homes and held struggle sessions against “reactionary academic authorities” early in the Cultural Revolution, many later became conservatives. Interpretation Li Xun citing discussions by Xu Youyu and Zhu Xueqin.

The scholar Andrew Walder divides such organizations into two kinds. One was formed by office staff protecting their own superiors. The other was made up of industrial workers in big cities, mobilized with help from Party organizations and the unions. The Shanghai Scarlet Guards were the second kind. Elizabeth Perry and Li Xun's Proletarian Power (《无产阶级的力量》) divides the actions of Shanghai workers in the Cultural Revolution into three kinds, rebellion, conservatism and economism. Conservatism was one kind of worker politics, with its own reasons.
895: People who came in looked for Commander Wang first. You shook hundreds of hands a day. Someone called you Commander Wang. You corrected them twice, and after that you stopped correcting them.
896: Pan Guoping sat behind the table in the middle of the inner room, and people who came in looked for Commander Pan first. You sat on his left. You handled organization, registration, and the newly carved official seal. When people came on business, once it was done, they would turn back on their way out and give you a nod.
897: A duty roster hung on the wall, the names of seven mills in a column. This week it was No. 31 State Cotton Mill's turn. Huang Jinhai sat behind the table in the middle. He was not used to it, and every so often he got up and walked a circle. Someone came in and asked who the commander was. He said there was no commander. The man paused, put his list on the table and left.
898: Someone at the registration desk read your name aloud, and someone beside him added, the one from the platform. No one laughed, and no one said anything more.
899: Some people also said behind your back, he came back halfway.
900: After Geng Jinzhang came back from Suzhou, he never set foot in these rooms. He hung up a sign of his own in Zhabei, and his men called him Commander Geng. He had someone pass you a message. Old Wang, come over for a drink when you have time.
901: The few hundred people from Kunshan later walked on to Suzhou and made Zhang Chunqiao sign again. A few days after they came back, they hung up a sign of their own in Zhabei. They called it the Second Regiment, and its leader was Geng Jinzhang of the Shanghai Pulp Mill. Some said he had been a Nationalist soldier. Some said he had been a deputy platoon leader and a Party member. His men called him Commander Geng.
902:
After the Five Demands were signed, the Workers' General Headquarters got a headquarters on Julu Road. Some time later it moved to Lane 1350, Middle Fuxing Road. There was a line at the door every day, all people coming to register. Some mills sent one representative with a stack of name lists in his pocket. Some people came alone and said they were the only one in their shop. The registration table was borrowed from a primary school, and other children's names were still carved into the top.

⟦0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧

At the end of November another sign went up, the Shanghai Headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards for Defending Mao Zedong Thought. Yang Shifa, head of the Municipal Organization Department, told them, this is what you should do. As he spoke he raised two clenched fists. You must get organized. The Municipal Federation of Trade Unions cleared an office for them. On December 6 they held their founding rally in People's Square, and Wang Shaoyong, an alternate secretary of the Municipal Party Committee, came and gave a speech of congratulations. A month before, you had waited at Culture Square for someone from the Municipal Party Committee until dark. They said they were the ones defending Chairman Mao, and the WGHQ was a gang who walked off the job and stopped trains. They outnumbered you. Many were Party and Youth League members, model workers, activists in the shops. Some said they had 800,000. The two loudest lines in their manifesto were “grasp revolution, promote production” and “use reason, not force.”

⟦4⟧

No. 17 State Cotton Mill set up Scarlet Guards too, led by Ma Ji. Like you he was a staff officer in the security section, two years older, and the two of you used to talk about everything. When you put up your first big-character poster in June, he was away on business in Qingdao. When he came back he wrote one of his own, questioning the deputy Party secretary. The two of you once went to the Textile Bureau together overnight to lodge a complaint. Then the work team came. He said the work team had been sent by the Party and he would help it. In October you pulled together a rebel team at the mill called the Yongzhong Team, and he pulled together a Defense Team. You wrote big-character posters about him, and he wrote one called “The Rebels in Our Mill,” saying that you talked about overthrowing the reactionary line while doing everything you could to get rid of Party leadership. That poster was copied many times. On November 25 the No. 17 Mill Scarlet Guards were founded, and four or five thousand people joined at once. Your rebel team had only a thousand-odd then.

On the day of the founding, at the mill gate, you saw the maintenance fitter from the fine-spinning shop, Master Qian, the one who spat in your face on October 10. He wore a new armband and stood in the front row, looking straight ahead. He did not look at you.

On the way home, Cui Gendi asked you something. Master Qian's wife worked in the same mill as her. Should she still talk to her from now on?
903: The few men who beat you at Kunshan Middle School all wore Second Regiment armbands now. When they saw you, one of them even nodded.
904: You said, speak when it is time to speak. Once you had said it, you were not sure yourself whether it was right.
